lras-s1.title: Resources and full-employment output in Country L

table.caption: Country L every ten years: labor force at full employment, machines and buildings, and full-employment real GDP (invented data for practice)

lras-s2.title: A year on the island of Tolva
lras-s2.text:
Tolva is an invented island nation. In one year:

  1. A hurricane destroys a fifth of Tolva's factories and its main power plant.
  2. Tolva finishes a new deep-water port that lets firms ship goods far more cheaply, for good.
  3. Tolva's households, cheered by a sports victory, spend more on restaurants and travel.

items.q: Using the table, calculate the percent change in Country L's full-employment real GDP from 2000 to 2010.

mistakes.why: 50 is the change in billions of dollars. The percent change divides it by the 2000 value: $\frac{50}{500} \times 100$.
You divided by the 2010 value. A percent change is measured from the earlier value, 500.

items.q: Based on the table, what happened to Country L's LRAS curve between 2010 and 2020?
options: It shifted left, as the stock of machines and buildings fell
It shifted right, because the labor force stayed at 22 million
It did not shift, because the labor force did not change
It moved down, because the price level fell

why.correct: LRAS sits at full-employment output. That output fell from 550 to 520 billion dollars, so LRAS shifted left.
options: Right: fewer capital goods lower full-employment output from 550 to 520, so LRAS shifts left.
An unchanged labor force does not raise potential output; capital fell, so LRAS shifted left.
LRAS depends on all resources and technology, and capital fell.
LRAS is vertical, so the price level does not move it. Its position is full-employment output.

items.q: Based on the table, in which ten years did Country L's LRAS shift right by the most?
options: No decade, because a vertical LRAS curve does not shift

why.correct: Compare full-employment real GDP: +50, -30, then +140. LRAS moved right by the most from 2020 to 2030.
options: LRAS shifted right then, but by 50 billion, less than the 140 billion of 2020 to 2030.
Right: full-employment output rose by 140 billion, as both labor and capital grew.
In those years full-employment output fell, so LRAS shifted left.
LRAS is vertical, but it shifts whenever full-employment output changes.

items.q: From 2020 to 2030, how would Country L's production possibilities curve (PPC) change, and why?
options: It would shift inward, because more of the resources are used
It would not change, because a PPC shows just two goods
It would shift outward, as labor and capital grew
The economy would move from a point inside the PPC to a point on it

why.correct: A rise in resources moves full-employment output and the PPC together: LRAS right, PPC out.
options: Using more resources does not shrink what can be made; more resources move the PPC out.
The PPC shows the limits on producing two goods, and those limits widen with more resources.
Right: LRAS shifting right and the PPC shifting out show the same rise in productive capacity.
That is a fall in unemployment of existing resources. Here the resources themselves grew.

items.q: How does event 1 (the hurricane) affect Tolva's LRAS?
options: LRAS shifts right, because rebuilding raises spending on new factories
LRAS is unaffected, because the labor force is the same
There is a movement along LRAS to a higher price level
LRAS shifts left, as Tolva has less capital to produce with

why.correct: The hurricane destroys capital, so the most Tolva can produce at full employment falls: LRAS shifts left.
options: Rebuilding is spending (AD); it does not add capacity until the factories are rebuilt.
Labor is one resource; Tolva also lost capital, which lowers what full employment can produce.
LRAS is vertical at full-employment output. A loss of factories moves its position.
Right: losing capital lowers full-employment output.

items.q: Which event shifts Tolva's LRAS to the right?
options: Event 2, the new port
Event 1, the hurricane
Event 3, the rise in household spending
Events 1 and 3 together

why.correct: A lasting improvement in infrastructure raises productive capacity, so full-employment output and LRAS rise.
options: Right: a lasting fall in shipping costs raises what Tolva's resources can produce.
Losing factories shifts LRAS left, not right.
More spending shifts AD. It does not add to resources or technology.
Neither raises capacity: one destroys capital and the other is spending.

items.q: Why does event 3, the rise in household spending, not shift Tolva's LRAS?
options: Household spending is too small a part of GDP to matter
Spending shifts AD; LRAS depends on resources and technology
Restaurants and travel are services, which do not count in GDP
LRAS shifts when the government acts, not when households do

why.correct: Spending is demand. Full-employment output comes from the quantity and quality of resources and technology.
options: Consumption is the largest part of spending. It still does not change productive capacity.
Right: spending shifts AD; LRAS is set by what full employment of resources can produce.
Services do count in GDP. The point is that spending does not create new resources.
Many private changes shift LRAS, such as new technology or a larger labor force.

items.q: Why is the long-run aggregate supply curve vertical?
options: In the long run firms are unable to raise their prices, so they stop expanding output
In the long run the economy runs out of extra workers, so firms stop hiring more
Wages and prices fully adjust, so output depends on resources, not the price level
In the long run demand for goods stops changing

why.correct: When wages and prices all adjust, a change in the price level changes costs as much as revenues, so output returns to potential: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output.
options: In the long run every price can change. It is because all prices and wages adjust that output does not respond.
Output can rise above full employment for a time. The curve is vertical because wages catch up in the long run.
Right: once nominal wages catch up with prices, a higher price level no longer makes more output profitable.
Demand changes in the long run too. The vertical curve is about supply once wages adjust.

items.q: The price level in an economy doubles, and over time every nominal wage and input price doubles too. What happens to real output in the long run?
options: It doubles, because prices doubled
It falls by half, because goods are twice as expensive
It rises above full employment for good
It stays at full-employment output

why.correct: In the long run, the price level and all input prices move together, so real output is at potential whatever the price level: that is LRAS.
options: Higher prices raise output only while wages are stuck. Once wages double too, output is back at potential.
Incomes doubled as well. In the long run, output is set by resources, not by the price level.
Output above full employment cannot last once wages and input prices adjust.
Right: costs rose as much as prices, so production is no more profitable than before.

items.q: Which of the following would shift a country's LRAS to the right? Select all that apply.
options: More adults join the labor force
Workers become more skilled through better training
Firms build more factories and machines
Consumers become more confident and spend more
The price level rises
Firms' wage contracts expire and are renegotiated

why.correct: LRAS moves with the quantity and quality of resources (labor, capital, land) and with technology.
options: Right: more labor raises full-employment output.
Right: higher-quality labor raises output per worker.
Right: more capital raises productive capacity.
More spending shifts AD, not LRAS.
LRAS is vertical; a change in the price level does not move it.
Renegotiating wages moves SRAS; it does not change resources or technology.

items.q: A country adopts a new technology that lets every factory produce more with the same workers and machines. Shift the long-run aggregate supply curve to show the effect on full-employment output.

why.correct: Better technology raises what full employment of resources can produce, so LRAS shifts right.

slips.AD: Technology changes what the economy can produce, not what people plan to buy, so it shifts LRAS, not AD.

items.q: An earthquake destroys many factories, roads and power lines, which raises costs now and lowers what the economy can produce at full employment. Shift every curve this changes.

why.correct: Lost capital lowers full-employment output (LRAS left) and raises production costs at every price level now (SRAS left).

key.because: the loss of factories, roads and power lines

slips.AD: The earthquake destroys productive capacity. That shifts the supply curves, not spending.

items.q: Country P makes wheat and cloth. Many skilled workers move to Country P and find jobs. Shift its production possibilities curve to show the change in what it can produce.

why.correct: More labor lets Country P make more of both goods: the PPC shifts out, as LRAS shifts right.

key.because: a rise in the labor force

items.q: How are a country's LRAS curve and its production possibilities curve (PPC) related?
options: Both show capacity: as LRAS shifts right, the PPC shifts out
When LRAS shifts right, the PPC shifts inward
LRAS shows planned spending, while the PPC shows production
They are unrelated, because a PPC is about two goods rather than total output

why.correct: A point on the PPC is full employment of resources; that output is where LRAS stands. Both move with resources and technology.
options: Right: more resources or better technology move both.
More capacity moves the PPC out, not in.
LRAS is supply: full-employment output. Spending is AD.
The two goods on a PPC stand for all the economy makes, and its frontier moves with LRAS.

items.q: Make it specific: explain why LRAS is vertical.

why.correct: In the long run nominal wages and input prices adjust to the price level, so output returns to full employment at any price level.

specific.frame: In the long run, nominal wages and input prices ___ with the price level, so a higher price level makes production ___ profitable. Real output stays at ___.
specific.model: In the long run, nominal wages and input prices adjust with the price level, so a higher price level makes production no more profitable than before. Because costs rise as much as prices, real output stays at full-employment output.

change.label: Wages and input prices
options: adjust
stay fixed

why.1: Fixed wages describe the short run. In the long run contracts are renegotiated.

because.label: Profitability
options: no more
much more

why.1: Costs rise as much as prices, so the extra profit disappears.

output.label: Output
options: full-employment output
a higher level each year the price level rises

why.1: A higher price level does not add resources, so output cannot stay above potential.

items.q: Full-employment real GDP in Country N is 800 billion dollars. Where does Country N's LRAS curve stand?
options: Horizontal at the current price level
Vertical at a real GDP of 800 billion dollars
Sloping up through 800 billion dollars
Vertical at whatever real GDP the economy produces this year

why.correct: LRAS stands at potential output (YF), here 800 billion dollars, whatever the price level.
options: LRAS is vertical, not horizontal: output, not the price level, is fixed in the long run.
Right: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output.
An upward slope describes SRAS. In the long run the curve is vertical.
Actual output can be above or below full employment. LRAS stands at full-employment output.
